text.p: Swarms of locusts attacking farms in the north and west of Honduras have prompted an official investigation into whether the crisis has reached plague proportions, officials here said on Thursday.
Farmers on the border of Guatemala and in the northern region of Cortes say millions of the three-inch long insects had destroyed fields of corn, and mango, cashew nut and coconut trees.
"There are so many hoppers that when they fly they block out the sun," said one farmer in the Cortes area.

"When they come they come in their millions and are capable of devouring entire crops and trees," said Honduras's agriculture director Avilio Cruz, adding an official had already been sent to the Santa Barbara region, close to the Guatemalan border.
"He will verify whether the quantities claimed by the farmers merit treating this as a plague," he said.
One farm owner, Isaac Jaar, said the locusts had demolished his fruit trees and a nearby oak forest.

The problem would be difficult to manage if the insects had already developed into their flying stage, making indiscriminate fumigation futile, he said, but Santa Barbara farmers and councils were planning to use insecticides.
Locusts frequently attack farms in the south of Honduras and in neighbouring El Salvador and Guatemala.
